plain_english: Maybe you're wondering who I mean by "busy men." Don't think I'm only talking about the lawyers who get chased out of court when the day ends, or those you see either proudly surrounded by their own clients or rudely pushed around by strangers during formal visits. I don't just mean those who drag them from home to wait around at their patron's door, or who use the praetor's auctions to make shameful profits that will eventually destroy them. Some people are busy even in their leisure time. In their country house or lying on their couch, completely alone, even though they've withdrawn from all society, they still manage to torment themselves. We shouldn't call such men's lives leisurely — their business is just being lazy.
original_excerpt: Perhaps you will ask me whom I mean by "busy men"? you need not think that I allude only to those who are hunted out of the courts of justice with dogs at the close of the proceedings, those whom you see either honourably jostled by a crowd of their own clients or contemptuously hustled in visits of ceremony by strangers, who call them away from home to hang about their patron's doors, or who make use of the praetor's sales by auction to acquire infamous gains which some day will prove their own ruin. Some men's leisure is busy: in their country house or on their couch, in complete solitude, even though they have retired from all men's society, they still continue to worry themselves: we ought not to say that such men's life is one of leisure, but their very business is sloth.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: Would you call a man lazy who spends hours fussing over his expensive bronze statues — things that are only valuable because a few collectors have gone crazy for them? A man who wastes most of his day staring at old metal plates? Who sits in the gym (how embarrassing that we've even imported our bad habits from abroad) watching boys wrestle? Who sorts his chained slaves into matching pairs by age and skin color? Who keeps trendy athletes like pets?
original_excerpt: Would you call a man idle who expends anxious finicking care in the arrangement of his Corinthian bronzes, valuable only through the mania of a few connoisseurs? and who passes the greater part of his days among plates of rusty metal? who sits in the palaestra (shame, that our very vices should be foreign) watching boys wrestling? who distributes his gangs of fettered slaves into pairs according to their age and colour? who keeps athletes of the latest fashion?
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: Do you really call these men busy? They spend hours at the barber's shop. They have him pluck out every hair that grew overnight. They hold serious discussions about each individual hair. They carefully arrange their scattered locks and force the ones that fall back onto their foreheads. Watch how angry they get if the barber makes one small mistake — as if he were cutting up a real man! See how furious they become if some of their precious hair gets cut too short, or if one section doesn't look perfect, or if their curls don't lie in perfect rows! Which of them wouldn't rather see the government collapse than have his hairstyle messed up? Who doesn't care more about how his head looks than his actual health? Who wouldn't choose a good appearance over real honor?
original_excerpt: Why, do you call those men idle, who pass many hours at the barber's while the growth of the past night is being plucked out by the roots, holding councils over each several hair, while the scattered locks are arranged in order and those which fall back are forced forward on to the forehead? How angry they become if the shaver is a little careless, as though he were shearing a _man_! what a white heat they work themselves into if some of their mane is cut away, if some part of it is ill-arranged, if all their ringlets do not lie in regular order! who of them would not rather that the state were overthrown than that his hair should be ruffled? who does not care more for the appearance of his head than for his health? who would not prefer ornament to honour?
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: Do you call these men idle — the ones who spend all their time on their hair and mirrors? What about those who devote their entire lives to writing songs, listening to music, and learning melodies? They twist their voices through pointless musical runs when nature meant them to sound best when used simply. Their fingers are always tapping out some tune they're thinking about. Even when they're called to handle serious or tragic business, you can hear them humming to themselves. These people aren't at leisure — they're busy with nonsense.
original_excerpt: Do you call these men idle, who make a business of the comb and looking-glass? what of those who devote their lives to composing, hearing, and learning songs, who twist their voices, intended by Nature to sound best and simplest when used straightforwardly, through all the turns of futile melodies: whose fingers are always beating time to some music on which they are inwardly meditating; who, when invited to serious and even sad business may be heard humming an air to themselves?—such people are not at leisure, but are busy about trifles.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: And their dinner parties? Good God, I can't call those relaxing either. Look at the anxious care they put into arranging the silverware. Watch how they fuss over the servants' uniforms. See how they hold their breath waiting for the cook to present the roast boar just right. Notice how the slave boys sprint to their tasks the moment they're signaled. Watch the skillful carving of birds into perfect portions. See the miserable young servants carefully cleaning up after drunk guests. Through all this, these hosts are trying to impress people with their refined taste and wealth. Their need to show off follows them so deeply into private life that they can't even eat or drink without putting on a performance.
original_excerpt: As for their banquets, by Hercules, I cannot reckon them among their unoccupied times when I see with what anxious care they set out their plate, how laboriously they arrange the girdles of their waiters' tunics, how breathlessly they watch to see how the cook dishes up the wild boar, with what speed, when the signal is given, the slave-boys run to perform their duties, how skilfully birds are carved into pieces of the right size, how painstakingly wretched youths wipe up the spittings of drunken men. By these means men seek credit for taste and grandeur, and their vices follow them so far into their privacy that they can neither eat nor drink without a view to effect.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: I wouldn't call those men idle either — the ones who get carried around in chairs and litters, who wait for their scheduled exercise time like it's a sacred ritual they can't skip. These are men who need someone else to tell them when to bathe, when to swim, when to eat. They've become so weakly pampered that they can't even figure out if they're hungry.
original_excerpt: Nor should I count those men idle who have themselves carried hither and thither in sedans and litters, and who look forward to their regular hour for taking this exercise as though they were not allowed to omit it: men who are reminded by some one else when to bathe, when to swim, when to dine: they actually reach such a pitch of languid effeminacy as not to be able to find out for themselves whether they are hungry.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: I once heard one of these pampered rich people—though I'm not sure we should call it luxury when someone has forgotten how to be human—ask his servants, "Am I sitting down?" They had just carried him from his bath and put him in his chair. Can you imagine? A man who doesn't know if he's sitting—do you think he knows if he's alive? If he can see? If he has any free time? I honestly can't decide what's worse: if he really didn't know, or if he was just pretending.
original_excerpt: I have heard one of these luxurious folk—if indeed, we ought to give the name of luxury to unlearning the life and habits of a man—when he was carried in men's arms out of the bath and placed in his chair, say inquiringly, "Am I seated?" Do you suppose that such a man as this, who did not know when he was seated, could know whether he was alive, whether he could see, whether he was at leisure? I can hardly say whether I pity him more if he really did not know or if he pretended not to know this.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: These people really do lose awareness of a lot of things. But they pretend to be even more oblivious than they actually are. They actually take pride in some of their flaws because they think these flaws prove how successful they are. They believe that only pathetic, worthless people pay attention to what they're doing. After seeing this, do you really think playwrights are making things up when they mock the wealthy in their comedies? I swear, they leave out more than they invent. In our age — which excels at nothing except creating new vices — so many unbelievable forms of corruption have emerged that you could actually criticize the playwrights for failing to keep up with reality.
original_excerpt: Such people do really become unconscious of much, but they behave as though they were unconscious of much more: they delight in some failings because they consider them to be proofs of happiness: it seems the part of an utterly low and contemptible man to know what he is doing. After this, do you suppose that playwrights draw largely upon their imaginations in their burlesques upon luxury: by Hercules, they omit more than they invent; in this age, inventive in this alone, such a number of incredible vices have been produced, that already you are able to reproach the playwrights with omitting to notice them.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12

plain_english: Can you imagine someone so corrupted by luxury that they need another person to tell them whether they're sitting down or not? This person is definitely not enjoying leisure. You need a different word for him: he's sick, or actually dead. Only someone who knows they're at leisure is truly at leisure. But this poor creature is barely alive if he needs someone else to tell him what position his body is in. How could such a person possibly manage his time?
original_excerpt: To think that there should be any one who had so far lost his senses through luxury as to take some one else's opinion as to whether he was sitting or not? This man certainly is not at leisure: you must bestow a different title on him: he is sick, or rather dead: he only is at leisure who feels that he is at leisure: but this creature is only half alive, if he wants some one to tell him what position his body is in. How can such a man be able to dispose of any time?
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 12
